## Animations

The animation below shows the catenary $y = c\cosh(x/c)$ alongside its parabolic approximation $y = x^2/(2c) + c$ as the sag parameter $c$ increases from 0.5 to 4. The catenary is the curve formed by a flexible cable hanging under gravity; the parabola is the first two terms of its Maclaurin series.

Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

### Case 1 — Catenary vs parabola approximation as $c$ varies

**Behavior:** For large $c$ (nearly taut cable), the two curves are nearly indistinguishable near $x=0$. For small $c$ (slack cable), the catenary climbs more steeply than the parabola and the two separate well inside the window: at $c=0.5$ the gap passes 0.1 at $|x|\approx0.73$, and the catenary leaves the top of the plot at $|x|\approx1.94$, the parabola at $|x|\approx3.39$. The catenary never lies below the parabola, since their difference $x^4/(24c^3)+x^6/(720c^5)+\cdots$ is positive for every $x\neq0$. The lowest point is always at $(0, c)$.

[Julia source](catenaryaa.jl)

![Catenary y=c cosh(x/c) compared with its parabolic approximation y=x^2/(2c)+c as c sweeps from 0.5 to 4; the two curves nearly coincide near the apex for large c](catenaryaa.gif)
